document.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Secretary's Fourth Restricted Session with Shevardnadze, March 23, 1988
document.authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
document.note: Shultz asks Shevardnadze for informal assurances that the Soviets will not criticize Pakistan for violating the Geneva Accords, since Pakistan was the only realistic supply route to the resistance. After a US caucus the US adds a demand for a moratorium on arms shipments, which Shevardnadze rejects, and he later expresses acute disappointment. Both sides move toward mutual restraint.

events.description: Fourth restricted session between the U.S. Secretary and Shevardnadze on ministerial dates, Iran-Iraq, Afghanistan and the joint statement.
Planned Moscow ministerial meeting, April 21-25 including travel outside Moscow.
Further ministerial meeting planned for mid-May with dates to be determined.

U.S. proposes a moratorium on arms shipments to Afghanistan during Soviet withdrawal plus three months, without prejudice to rights to supply. Shevardnadze says agreement is not possible on that basis.
Shevardnadze states the USSR would not claim an accords violation if the U.S. continued supporting the resistance, though it would criticize it.
The Secretary took a ten-minute caucus with Powell, Armacost, Ridgway and Parris in his private office before restating the U.S. position.
Fourth restricted session between Shultz and Shevardnadze; US proposes arms moratorium and guarantor role on Afghanistan, Soviets reject.
Shevardnadze says Geneva accords could be signed without guarantors and the US would remain outside the settlement.
Fourth restricted session between Secretary Shultz and Shevardnadze, covering Afghanistan, Cambodia and Korea.
Shevardnadze says the US would not act as guarantor for the Geneva accords, so the USSR would not either; the guarantee language would be deleted.
Shevardnadze states Vietnam would have withdrawn its troops from Cambodia by 1990.
Secretary Shultz's fourth restricted session with Shevardnadze in Washington; discussion of Nicaragua, regional dialogue, Iran-Iraq, Afghanistan, Cambodia.
Shevardnadze says there was no progress on Afghanistan and that the U.S. pulled back from its commitments.

Shevardnadze concludes the U.S. would not act as guarantor of the Geneva accords, so the USSR would not either; the Secretary says the U.S. was ready to sign in Geneva subject to a workable formula and proposes a moratorium on arms supplies.
Shevardnadze states Vietnam would withdraw its troops from Cambodia by 1990.
Shultz's fourth restricted session with Shevardnadze in Moscow, discussing Afghanistan arms supplies and the Geneva accords.
Shultz phoned Sen. Byrd, who worried about giving away Afghanistan.
Shultz held a ten-minute private caucus with Powell, Armacost, Ridgway and Parris, then outlined the U.S. position.
Shevardnadze said the USSR would not claim a violation of the Geneva accords if the U.S. continued aid, though it would criticize it. Signing was still days away.
Shultz's fourth restricted session with Shevardnadze covering dates, Iran-Iraq, Afghanistan.
Agreed April ministerial meeting in Moscow, April 21-25, with Shultz discussions April 21-22.
Ministers to meet in mid-May, dates to be determined.
Shevardnadze confirmed the Soviet Union would act in the UN Security Council on Iran-Iraq after the Secretary General's consultations; 'strong action' to appear in joint statement.
Shevardnadze indicated Moscow would not invent a complaint over Pakistan if there were no actual act of supply of arms to the resistance.
Shultz's fourth restricted session with Shevardnadze covering Central America, arms supplies and regional dialogue including Afghanistan.
Shevardnadze raised the question of limiting naval activities the day before.
Yazov showed Carlucci a map of U.S. bases ringing the Soviet Union.
Ceasefire talks between the Sandinista government and the contras began under the Guatemala City accords, with a Soviet aircraft in Nicaragua cited by the U.S.
Gorbachev was in Washington for the summit and said the Soviet Union supported the Guatemala City accords and Contadora, and offered to cut Nicaragua aid.
The U.S. dispatched troops to Honduras, criticized by Shevardnadze.
Series of U.S.-Nicaragua bilateral meetings at Manzanillo supporting the Contadora process, later broken off by the U.S.
Sandinista revolution ousted Somoza and the U.S. welcomed it and gave economic assistance.
Shultz–Shevardnadze fourth restricted session discussing Afghanistan, Central America.
Secretary caucused ten minutes in private office with Powell, Armacost, Ridgway, Parris, then outlined US position.
US proposed a moratorium on arms shipments during Soviet withdrawal plus three months; Soviets rejected it; US conditioned guarantor role on it.
Ministers discussed basic elements of Central America issue Monday evening.
Nicaraguan troops (1,500-2,000) moved into Honduras; US sent forces in show of support, expected to return home over the weekend.

key_claims: The U.S. wanted to keep the right to arm the Afghan resistance after the Geneva accords while avoiding Soviet charges that Pakistan violated them.
Shevardnadze said the accords imposed no obligation on guarantors not to supply arms, so the USSR would criticize but not claim a violation by the U.S.
The U.S. noted Pakistan was the only realistic route for supplies to the resistance, making its position central.
Shevardnadze said Pakistan was bound not to supply the opposition and UN inspectors would monitor it.
The U.S. proposed a moratorium on arms shipments during the Soviet withdrawal plus three months, and Shevardnadze rejected it on that basis.
The Soviets agreed to withdraw half their troops within three months of the accords and finish within the year, with Cordovez mediating an interim government.
Congressional pressure (Sen. Byrd) constrained the U.S. posture on signing the Geneva accords.
The US proposed a moratorium on arms to Afghan parties during the Soviet withdrawal and three months after, and offered to be guarantor of the Geneva accords only if accepted.
Shevardnadze rejected the moratorium, saying Geneva accords could be signed without guarantors or at all.
Soviets insisted on the right to keep supplying the Kabul regime and objected to equating it with fundamentalist bands.
The US said Pakistan would make its own decisions and wanted Geneva signed.
Shevardnadze accused the US of backing away from commitments on Afghanistan and said confidence was shaken.
The US pressed 'symmetry' in outside supply, which Shevardnadze rejected as equating the Kabul government with fundamentalist bands.
The US proposed a moratorium on supplies, or a Kabul-initiated call for one, as an alternative to Soviet resupply before the Geneva accords entered into force.
Shevardnadze concluded the US would stay outside the Afghan settlement process and would not guarantee the Geneva accords, so the USSR would not either.
Both sides acknowledged Pakistan would make its own decisions on the Geneva accords.
Shevardnadze linked Afghan national reconciliation to prospects for settlements in Cambodia and southern Africa.
